items.title: Shingles and seal strips

children.text: Asphalt shingles resist wind largely through the factory sealant that bonds each course to the one below. Once that bond breaks, wind gets under the shingle and works on the nails. Many wind-damaged roofs have no missing shingles at all.

items.description: Asphalt shingles resist wind largely through the factory sealant that bonds each course to the one below. Once that bond breaks, wind gets under the shingle and works on the nails. Many wind-damaged roofs have no missing shingles at all.
items.label: Discuss an Inspection

cards.title: Broken seal strips
cards.description: A shingle can look flat and still be unsealed.

children.text: Why the bond matters IBHS notes that wind can lift unsealed shingles and let water seep underneath. New shingles can take one to two months or more to seal in poor conditions. We check courses by hand on the windward slopes, where wind usually breaks the most bonds. A shingle that lifts freely along a whole course points to a wider bond failure, not a single loose piece.

cards.title: Creased shingles
cards.description: When wind lifts a shingle and drops it, the mat can fold across the nail line.

children.text: Why a crease counts as damage A crease is a break in the shingle's mat. It won't lie flat again or reseal reliably. Creases usually run in a line across several shingles on the same course. Creased shingles are replaced. Gluing them down leaves the fold in place.

cards.title: Missing shingles and exposed nails
cards.description: A blown-off shingle leaves nail heads and the course above it exposed.

children.text: What sits under the gap Exposed nails and nail holes let water track down into the underlayment and deck. We check whether the shingles around the gap were nailed correctly, because nail position affects how a shingle holds in wind. Underlayment and decking under the opening are checked before new shingles go on.

cards.title: Granules and scuffs
cards.description: Bare spots and fresh scuffs show where shingles flapped or debris dragged.

children.text: How we read them A heavy pile of granules at the downspouts after a storm is worth mentioning when you call. Scuffs alone may be cosmetic. Scuffs with lifted or creased shingles usually aren't. Hail leaves a different pattern. See
hail damage roof repair
if the storm brought both.

items.title: Ridges, edges, flashing and gutters

children.text: Wind loads are highest at the roof's edges, corners and ridge, so failures often start there before reaching the shingle field.

items.description: Wind loads are highest at the roof's edges, corners and ridge, so failures often start there before reaching the shingle field.

groups.title: Ridges, edges, flashing and gutters — Details

cards.title: Ridge and hip caps
cards.description: Ridge caps sit on the most exposed line of the roof.

children.text: What fails and how it's fixed Caps crack or blow off, exposing the ridge vent or the shingle tops underneath. Hip and ridge caps are made to bend over the seam and are fastened on each side above the sealant strip. A lost run of caps is replaced with a compatible cap product, and the ridge vent is checked for wind damage.

cards.title: Eaves and rakes
cards.description: Wind gets under the first course at the eaves and along the gable rakes.

children.text: Why the edge needs attention IBHS says the starter strip helps prevent water intrusion and protects against wind uplift at the roof edges. We check the starter course, the drip edge and the first shingle course for lifting. An edge that was never properly started tends to fail again. The estimate should say how the new edge will be built.

cards.title: Flashing
cards.description: Wind loosens step flashing, counterflashing and chimney flashing, opening a path for water.

children.text: What we check Step flashing along walls and dormers, chimney flashing and counterflashing, skylight and vent flanges Bent, lifted or face-caulked pieces are reset or replaced, not coated over The repair names the failed part rather than treating everything as a shingle replacement

cards.title: Gutters and downspouts
cards.description: Wind and falling limbs pull gutters away from the fascia and bend downspouts.

children.text: Gutters belong in the same inspection Gutters pulled from the fascia can let water behind them onto the fascia board and the roof edge. We note gutter and fascia damage separately on the estimate, not folded into the roof patch. Gutter repair and replacement are covered on our

cards.title: ASTM D3161 (Class A, D, F)
cards.description: A fan-driven test of shingles on a test deck.

children.text: What the class means IBHS describes D3161 as measuring a shingle's ability to withstand fan-induced wind speeds. Class F is the highest D3161 class. GAF lists it as 110 mph. The speed describes air flowing over the shingles in the lab, not the wind load on your house.

cards.title: ASTM D7158 (Class D, G, H)
cards.description: An uplift test that measures how strongly the sealed shingle resists being pulled up.

children.text: What the class means IBHS: D7158 assigns a class based on a two-part uplift test, and the classes tie to ASCE 7 wind zones. Class H is the highest D7158 class. GAF lists it as 150 mph. Both tests evaluate new product. IBHS notes they don't account for weathering or aging. An older roof doesn't keep its rating.

cards.title: Wind warranty is a separate promise

children.text: What usually decides coverage The stated mph applies to a particular product, installed a particular way. Higher wind coverage often requires the manufacturer's starter, ridge and other accessories, extra nails or a special application. The product cards below show each line's conditions. Shingles generally need to have sealed. Damage from falling trees or debris is a different matter from blow-off. Your proposal names the product, and the manufacturer's warranty document sets the terms.

items.question: How strong does wind have to be to damage a roof?

children.text: There's no single number. Shingle age, how well the courses sealed, nailing, roof shape and exposure all matter. Wind ratings are measured on new shingles in a lab, and IBHS notes the tests don't account for weathering or aging. Older roofs, edges and ridges usually fail first. After any storm that sends shingles into the yard, have the roof checked.

items.question: Can a few blown-off shingles be repaired, or does the whole roof need replacing?

children.text: Most wind damage is repairable. A repair makes sense when the damage is confined to identifiable areas and the surrounding shingles still seal and bend without cracking. Replacement belongs in the conversation when seal strips have failed across whole slopes or the old shingles are too brittle to work. You'll get the reason in writing either way. See
roof repair
for repairs beyond storm damage.

items.question: Will new shingles match the rest of my roof?

children.text: Often closely, but rarely perfectly. Weathering, color batches and discontinued lines all affect the match. How that applies to your roof is the insurer's call.

Once the tree is off, the roof inspection should check the decking and framing under the impact, not just the shingles.

Asphalt shingles resist wind largely through the factory sealant that bonds each course to the one below. Once that bond breaks, wind gets under the shingle and works on the nails. Many wind-damaged roofs have no missing shingles at all.

Why the bond matters IBHS notes that wind can lift unsealed shingles and let water seep underneath. New shingles can take one to two months or more to seal in poor conditions. We check courses by hand on the windward slopes, where wind usually breaks the most bonds. A shingle that lifts freely along a whole course points to a wider bond failure, not a single loose piece.

Why a crease counts as damage A crease is a break in the shingle's mat. It won't lie flat again or reseal reliably. Creases usually run in a line across several shingles on the same course. Creased shingles are replaced. Gluing them down leaves the fold in place.

What sits under the gap Exposed nails and nail holes let water track down into the underlayment and deck. We check whether the shingles around the gap were nailed correctly, because nail position affects how a shingle holds in wind. Underlayment and decking under the opening are checked before new shingles go on.

Wind loads are highest at the roof's edges, corners and ridge, so failures often start there before reaching the shingle field.

What fails and how it's fixed Caps crack or blow off, exposing the ridge vent or the shingle tops underneath. Hip and ridge caps are made to bend over the seam and are fastened on each side above the sealant strip. A lost run of caps is replaced with a compatible cap product, and the ridge vent is checked for wind damage.

Why the edge needs attention IBHS says the starter strip helps prevent water intrusion and protects against wind uplift at the roof edges. We check the starter course, the drip edge and the first shingle course for lifting. An edge that was never properly started tends to fail again. The estimate should say how the new edge will be built.

What we check Step flashing along walls and dormers, chimney flashing and counterflashing, skylight and vent flanges Bent, lifted or face-caulked pieces are reset or replaced, not coated over The repair names the failed part rather than treating everything as a shingle replacement

We note gutter and fascia damage separately on the estimate, not folded into the roof patch. Gutter repair and replacement are covered on ourgutter services page .

Both tests evaluate new product. IBHS notes they don't account for weathering or aging. An older roof doesn't keep its rating.

Higher wind coverage often requires the manufacturer's starter, ridge and other accessories, extra nails or a special application. The product cards below show each line's conditions. groups.title: Deductibles, depreciation and what the insurer pays — Details

cards.title: Your deductible
cards.description: The deductible is the part of a covered loss you pay. Some policies set a separate wind, hail or roof deductible.

children.text: Be cautious with any offer to cover or waive your insurance deductible. The reason: the insurer pays from the price it's told. In Ohio, knowingly presenting a false or misleading statement to an insurer to defraud it is insurance fraud. If paying the deductible is the problem, see financing below.
Read Ohio’s Property Claim Rules

cards.title: Actual cash value (ACV)
cards.description: ACV pays the roof's replacement cost minus depreciation for age and wear.

children.text: Ohio's claims rule: the insurer determines actual cash value from the replacement cost at the time of loss, including sales tax, less depreciation, and must give you documentation of the depreciation on request. NAIC's illustration: $15,000 of roof damage with $10,000 of depreciation and a $1,000 deductible pays $4,000 under ACV, against $14,000 under replacement cost. Illustrative figures, not a Roof King price.
Read Ohio’s Property Claim Rules

cards.title: Replacement cost value (RCV)
cards.description: RCV pays to repair or replace the roof without subtracting depreciation, less your deductible.

children.text: Insurers often pay the actual cash value first and reimburse the withheld amount, called recoverable depreciation, after the work is done and the invoice is submitted. That's how North Carolina's insurance regulator describes it; check your own policy for the process and the deadline.
Read Ohio’s Property Claim Rules

cards.title: Matching new shingles to the old
cards.description: For applicable replacement-cost settlements under Ohio’s rule, matching should produce a reasonably comparable appearance. How the rule applies depends on the covered loss and policy.

children.text: Our estimate names the shingle line on your roof where it can be identified, so you can raise matching with your insurer. Lines shown on our site are below.

cards.title: Upgrades you choose

faq.title: Roof Insurance Claim Questions

items.question: Can Roof King file or negotiate my insurance claim?

children.text: No. You file the claim and deal with your insurer. Ohio requires a public adjuster license to negotiate or settle a claim for compensation, and ODI advises homeowners not to let a contractor do it. We inspect, document the damage and explain the process so you can make your own decisions.

items.question: Should I call my insurer or a roofer first?

children.text: Contact your insurer promptly; Columbus warns that claims often have reporting deadlines. An inspection helps you see whether the damage likely exceeds your deductible. Whether to file a claim is your decision, and we'll give you clear information to make it.

items.question: Will you cover or waive my deductible?

children.text: Be cautious with any contractor who offers to. The deductible is your share of a covered loss, and misleading an insurer about the price is insurance fraud in Ohio. Financing can spread the cost: 3- or 5-year options on qualifying projects, subject to lender approval and applicable terms.

items.question: What's the difference between ACV and replacement cost on a roof claim?

children.text: Actual cash value is the replacement cost minus depreciation; Ohio's rule lets you ask for documentation of every depreciation deduction. Replacement cost pays without subtracting depreciation, less your deductible, though insurers often hold part back until the work is finished.

items.question: How long does an Ohio insurer have to respond to my claim?

children.text: Under Ohio's claims rule, 15 days to acknowledge it, and 21 days from a properly executed proof of loss to accept or deny it. If it needs longer, it must tell you why and update you in writing at least every 45 days.

items.question: What if the insurer's estimate is lower than yours?

children.text: Compare them line by line. If items are missing, send the insurer our photos and estimate and ask, in writing, for a re-inspection or revised estimate. We explain our findings; the amount is settled between you and your insurer.

items.question: My claim was denied. What now?

children.text: Read the policy provision the denial cites; Ohio requires the insurer to name it. Ask ODI's consumer services team (800-686-1526) about your options, or consider a licensed public adjuster or attorney. You can still repair the damage, with financing if needed.

items.question: Can I trust a contractor who knocks on my door after a storm?

children.text: Check before you sign. ODI recommends verifying registration with the Ohio Secretary of State, getting more than one estimate and watching any inspection. Columbus residents can also look up licensed contractors on the City's Citizen Access Portal.

editorial.pageTitle: Roof Insurance Claims, Columbus OH | Roof King & Restoration

children.text: A roof insurance claim and the roof repair rest on the same facts: what the storm damaged, where and when. Roof King & Restoration inspects the roof, siding and gutters, documents the damage clearly and explains the insurance process so you can decide whether a claim makes sense. You file the claim and speak with your insurer, and your insurer decides coverage and payment.
Water coming in now? Call (614) 379-8893, describe the active problem and ask about current availability.

sections.title: Who Does What in an Ohio Roof Claim

children.text: Clear responsibilities help keep construction findings separate from policy decisions.

You report the claim, speak with your insurer and authorize the repair. Keep the policy, photos, correspondence and written proposals together. Avoid blank or incomplete contracts and record payments.

Your insurer investigates, decides coverage under the policy and handles payment. Ohio generally requires acknowledgement within 15 calendar days and an accept-or-deny decision within 21 days of properly executed proof of loss. If additional investigation is needed, the insurer must explain within that period and provide written status updates at least every 45 days.
Ohio’s Claim Acknowledgement and Investigation Rules

We inspect, document the observed condition, explain the construction findings and build the work you authorize. We do not negotiate or settle insurance claims. Paid public adjusting requires the applicable Ohio authority.
Ohio Public Insurance Adjuster Definitions
Ohio Public Adjuster Authority Requirement

sections.title: Paying for What Insurance Doesn’t Cover

children.text: Even an approved claim can leave part of the cost with you. Plan for these items before work begins:
Your policy deductible.
Depreciation not payable under an actual-cash-value roof settlement.
Upgrades you choose beyond the covered replacement.
Items the insurer declines, or the repair if a claim is denied.
Recoverable depreciation that may be withheld until completed repairs are documented.

If removal reveals damaged decking or another concealed condition, the additional work should be documented, priced and approved before proceeding. Construction findings are not an insurer’s agreement to pay.

Identify the shingle line, profile, finish and related flashings. Discuss aging, discontinued products and how close a replacement can match the retained roof. Include the adjoining repairs needed to restore the affected connection.

Review the written contract before work begins, including payment stages and the completion record. For covered Ohio home-solicitation sales, the cancellation period generally runs until midnight of the third business day after signing; the applicable agreement and statutory rules govern.
Ohio Home-Solicitation Cancellation Rules

children.text: Ground observations cannot establish every roof condition. Describe the storm, any new symptoms and previous repairs when requesting an assessment. Avoid climbing onto the roof to investigate.

items.question: Does temporary protection finish the job?

children.text: No. It is intended to limit exposure while the permanent repair plan is established. Confirm the area covered, its limitations and the remaining repair work.
